docs.title: Aiculator
docs.text:
Run a queue of coding tasks across AI harnesses, from one binary. Aiculator gives each task to an agent of the right tier, isolates the work in a git worktree, runs the acceptance checks itself, and merges what passes.

An agent saying "done" counts for nothing. The swarm verifies every result on its own.

A real server doing real work, from scripts/screenshots.sh. Agents were driven through the CLI, so the token and cost figures are demo values.

Get started See what is built

docs.title: Connect a project and finish a task
docs.text:
$ aiculator join --tier 1
Skills are in .agents/skills. Edit them only there.

claude     MCP in .mcp.json after a restart; shell works now
           Claude Code does not read .agents/skills, so it gets a link. It asks you to approve .mcp.json in interactive sessions.

In a NEW session, ask it to use the swarm-join skill (/swarm-join in Claude Code).
In a session ALREADY OPEN, paste this; it needs no restart:

  Read .agents/skills/swarm-join/SKILL.md and follow it. Join as tier 1.

$ aiculator task add --title "Add a health endpoint" \
    --spec "Add GET /healthz returning 200." --check "go test ./..."

An agent picks the task up, works in its own worktree, and submits. The swarm then runs go test ./... itself, in a sandbox, on a clean checkout. Only then does the work land on swarm/integration. Your own branches are never touched.

$ aiculator task ls
ID          STATE     TIER TRIES OWNER          TITLE
j1          done      1    1                    Create note1.txt
j2          done      1    1                    Create note2.txt
j3          done      1    1                    Create note3.txt

docs.text:
aiculator top shows flow, throughput, latency with jitter, health probes, usage and which tasks are in trouble. It runs on its own with no setup.

TasksUsage and budgetsFlow

docs.title: Or in your browser, including on a phone

$ aiculator web

docs.title: Turn a harness you already have open into a worker
docs.text:
Paste one line into any session, with no restart:

Read .agents/skills/swarm-join/SKILL.md and follow it. Join as tier 1.

Or launch sandboxed workers that use no model turns while idle:

SWARM_TOKEN=$(aiculator token --agent worker1 --tier 1) \
  aiculator drive --harness claude --agent worker1

docs.title: Keep waiting agents informed while planning
docs.text:
$ aiculator plan begin --ttl 5m
{ "epoch": 1 }
$ aiculator plan update --epoch 1 --ttl 5m --phase "splitting the spec" --expected 1=8 --expected 2=2

Every waiting agent now gets this, so it knows whether to keep waiting or leave:

{
  "action": "wait",
  "reason": "planning",
  "planning": { "epoch": 1, "phase": "splitting the spec", "expected_tasks": { "1": 8, "2": 2 } }
}

docs.title: Write instructions once, with templates
docs.text:
Reusable blocks for the rules you keep repeating. This template:

<Subagents use="when" max="4" when="the work splits into independent parts"
  not_when="the steps depend on each other" />

<Backoff timeout="120s" retries="2" />

<Flow name="confirm before acting">
<Step n="1" title="Plan" ask="Does this plan look right?"
  subagent="Do not ask. Continue, and report your plan with the result.">
List the changes you intend to make.
</Step>
</Flow>

Renders to plain instructions, with the retry waits worked out and a contents list whose line numbers let a model jump straight to a section:

## Contents

- Subagents: line 28, anchor `subagents`
- Commands: timeouts and retries: line 39, anchor `backoff`

## Commands: timeouts and retries

Give every command a time limit of **120s**. A command that hits the limit has failed; do not wait longer.

| Attempt | Wait before it |
|---|---|
| 1 | None |
| 2 | 2s |
| 3 | 4s |

docs.title: Make a model ask with a list, not a paragraph
docs.text:
Templates for single-choice lists, checkboxes, tabbed forms, staged subagent flows, and sections a model keeps current. On a real model, ui-tabs produced one call with three questions:

Language  one of: Go (Recommended), TypeScript, Python
Database  one of: PostgreSQL (Recommended), SQLite, MongoDB, None
Hosting   one of: Fly.io (Recommended), AWS, Render, Self-hosted VPS

See Templates, or the template demo, which uses every feature at once.

docs.title: Debug it the way you debug Kubernetes
docs.text:
$ aiculator task ls -v=6
level=INFO msg=request v=6 component=client method=GET url=http://127.0.0.1:7777/v1/tasks status=200 took=1.1ms bytes=2

$ aiculator debug verbosity 5 --for 10m     # Trace a running server, then go back by itself
$ aiculator logs -f --component engine

Levels 0 to 9 mean what they mean in kubectl, and credentials never reach a log at any level. See Debugging.

docs.title: Why it holds up
docs.text:
What it does How that was checked Survives crashes. Nothing acknowledged is lost. 100 real kill -9 crashes in every test run, checking about 65,000 acknowledged writes Never hands a task to two agents. Porcupine linearizability checks, and TLA+ models of crashes and lost replies Catches zombies and liars. Fake agents that crash, hang or lie about being done Stays fast. A wake takes 0.32 ms at p99, and a grant with 20,000 tasks queued takes 32 µs. Performance budgets in CI Contains agents. Real sandbox escape attempts on macOS and Linux Stays small. Archives are under 11 MiB. A size budget every build enforces

Early software

This is version 0.1. Only Claude Code and OpenCode have been run end to end, and several planned features are not built. See Status for exactly what works.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Aiculator is one Go binary with embedded NATS JetStream. It needs no external services.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Channels
        MCP[MCP tools]
        SH[Shell: aiculator work]
        ACP[ACP driver]
        HTTP[HTTP API]
    end
    subgraph Core
        W[Single writer and dispatcher]
        SM[Pure state machine]
        KV[(Task KV)]
        EV[(Event log)]
    end
    subgraph Work
        WT[Git worktrees]
        CH[Sandboxed checks]
        MQ[Merge queue]
    end
    MCP --> W
    SH --> HTTP --> W
    ACP --> HTTP
    W --> SM
    W -->|compare-and-swap| KV
    KV -->|projector| EV
    W --> WT
    W --> CH --> MQ
    MQ --> B[swarm/integration]

docs.title: The commit path
docs.text:
One goroutine owns all task state:

  1. A command reaches the writer, and a pure function, core.Apply, checks that it is legal.
  2. The writer makes one compare-and-swap write to the task's key. This is the commit point.
  3. Only after that write is acknowledged does it wake whoever is waiting.
  4. A projector follows the KV stream and writes the event log, using task:revision as the message ID so that replays are safe.

Since there is only one commit point, a crash cannot leave the state and the log disagreeing for good. Everything else in memory is rebuilt from KV on startup.

docs.title: Dispatch
docs.text:
wait_for_task returns a task already leased to the agent, so there is no second round trip and nothing to race for. New tasks wake only as many agents as there are tasks.

Priority aging needs no re-sorting. Each ready task has a fixed key, priority times the aging unit minus the time it became ready, and comparing those keys gives the same order as comparing priority plus waiting time at any moment.

docs.title: Channels hold no state
docs.text: MCP, the shell commands and the ACP driver all call the same service, so they behave the same. Agent identity always comes from a signed token and never from a request's arguments.

docs.title: Leases run on the writer's clock
docs.text: The NATS per-key TTL can be set only when a key is created, and a fake clock cannot control it. So leases run on the writer's own clock, which makes them testable. The TTL is used only to show which agents are around.

docs.title: Worktrees and saved work
docs.text: Each attempt gets its own worktree. The swarm saves work under refs/swarm/<task>/, using a private index so that it does not disturb the agent's staged files. A new attempt starts from the saved work and merges in whatever has landed since.

docs.title: The sandbox
docs.text:
aiculator drive and all acceptance checks run sandboxed. auto picks Seatbelt on macOS and bubblewrap on Linux, and falls back to Docker. If none is available, it fails: running without a sandbox must be asked for by name, with --sandbox none.

A sandboxed command Can it? Write to its worktree and private temp directory Yes Write anywhere else, including the repository's .git No Read the swarm's admin token and signing key No Read ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, ~/.gnupg and similar No Inherit your environment variables No, only what the manifest names Use the network Workers yes, because models need it. Checks no.

How well each sandbox is tested

Seatbelt and bubblewrap are attacked for real in the test suite, including escapes through symlinks. For Docker, only the arguments have been checked so far.

docs.title: Identity
docs.text:
Agent tokens are signed with ed25519. Tier and identity come from the token, so an agent cannot claim a higher tier or act as another agent. No token can be issued for the swarm's own system: identities.

Viewer tokens are read-only and expire, for dashboards and scrapers. See Dashboards.

docs.title: Verification rules
docs.text:
These are enforced by the state machine and modeled in TLA+:

  • A submitter cannot review its own work.
  • A task reaches done only after someone other than its submitter has verified it.
  • A reviewer cannot approve work whose checks have not passed.
  • An agent with an old lease cannot change a task.

docs.title: Untrusted text
docs.text: Notes from other agents and check output are marked as untrusted when shown to a model. This reduces prompt injection, but it cannot rule it out, which is one more reason results are checked by running them.

docs.title: What is not protected
docs.text:
A session joined by hand is not sandboxed

It runs under your harness's own permissions, and it can read the admin token, as you can. Treat it as you would yourself. Only checks run sandboxed in that case.

  • The server is for one trusted user on localhost, and is not hardened for a shared network.
  • Harness packages run with npx are pinned to a version, but you are still trusting what that version does.

See SECURITY.md in the repository for how to report a vulnerability.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> draft
    draft --> ready: published
    ready --> claimed: granted
    claimed --> running: first heartbeat or progress
    claimed --> ready: timeout or release
    claimed --> review: submit
    running --> review: submit
    running --> failed: fail or timeout
    running --> ready: release
    review --> merging: verified
    review --> failed: checks or review failed
    merging --> done: merged
    merging --> failed: merge conflict
    failed --> ready: retry or escalate
    failed --> parked: out of tiers or budget
    parked --> ready: unpark
    done --> [*]
    canceled --> [*]

Any state except done can also move to canceled.

docs.title: Tiers
docs.text:
A tier is a number, and which model counts as which tier is your choice, set in the agent's token.

Tier Typical work Takes lower-tier tasks 1 Standard Mechanical edits, tests, docs None lower 2 Advanced Multi-file features, debugging, reviews Tier 1 tasks, after 2 minutes 3 Ultra Architecture and the hardest problems Tier 2 tasks, after 5 minutes

Eligibility also needs the task's tags, and no overlap between its --touches paths and those of work in progress.

docs.title: What happens on failure
docs.text:
1. Two failures raise the task's tier.
  2. The next attempt inherits the saved work and the earlier notes, marked as untrusted.
  3. After the top tier fails twice, the task is parked with the reason needs_resplit, for a human or a planner.

A task that goes over its budget is parked with budget_exhausted. aiculator task unpark ID --add-budget N returns it to the queue.

A claim that times out before work starts costs nothing, and neither does a release.

docs.title: Zombies
docs.text: A heartbeat shows only that an agent is alive. Progress is measured separately: the swarm hashes the worktree itself, and only a changed hash counts. An agent with a live heartbeat and unchanged files loses its lease when the progress timeout runs out, which is 10 minutes by default. Its late submit is refused, and its saved work goes to the next attempt.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Run the whole set with:

go test -race ./...     # Includes the crash test
./scripts/formal.sh     # TLA+ and Alloy; needs Java

docs.title: Crash testing
docs.text:
TestKill9Gate starts a real server process, hammers it from several clients, and kills it with SIGKILL at a random moment, 100 times. After every restart it checks that:

  • Every stored task is valid.
  • Nothing a client was told succeeded has been lost.
  • No lease number was ever granted twice.

Power loss is a separate question

kill -9 does not test it, because written data survives in the page cache. Use aiculator serve --sync-always if you need that, at some cost in speed.

docs.title: Linearizability
docs.text: Porcupine checks that concurrent operations behave like one sequential FIFO queue. A second test confirms the checker catches a deliberately broken history, so that a pass means something.

docs.title: Formal models
docs.text:
Model What it proves spec/tla/Swarm.tla Unique leases, fencing against zombies, and done always means independently verified, across crashes and lost replies spec/tla/SwarmLiveness.tla A task always ends done or parked, even with hostile agents, if an agent that keeps getting chances eventually finishes spec/tla/Planner.tla An agent told to exit never misses work from that plan spec/alloy/swarm.als Tier and tag eligibility, plan deadlocks, and file lease conflicts

Models named Bug break a rule on purpose and must fail, which proves the checker can catch that defect. The planner model found a real bug: agents could exit on a hint of no work, and then the planner could add work anyway.

What these results do not say

They are bounded: they hold for the models at the sizes in each .cfg file and check command. Only the transition table is tied to the code automatically, by TestSpecMatchesCode. The other rules were written by hand from the code, and the tests have to cover that gap.

docs.title: Performance budgets
docs.text:
go test -run TestPerf ./internal/engine ./cmd/aiculator holds the code to these budgets, and CI runs it on every push. The cases are deliberately large, to expose work that grows badly with the number of tasks. Budgets leave room for a busy CI machine, so a failure means a real regression.

What Measured on an M-series Mac Budget Add a task and wake a waiting agent, p99 0.32 ms 5 ms, or 50 ms in CI One add-and-grant cycle 55 µs, about 18,000 per second 2 ms One grant among 32 competing agents 18 µs 2 ms Grant with 20,000 tasks waiting, p99 32 µs 10 ms Wake with 2,000 agents waiting, p99 0.78 ms 25 ms One plan_add with 5,000 drafts 0.15 ms 3 ms Commit a 5,000-task plan 44 ms 1 s Restart with 20,000 tasks 0.31 s 5 s Dashboard snapshot with 20,000 tasks, p99 6 ms 100 ms Heap per task 1.3 KiB 16 KiB CLI start 9 ms 200 ms Server ready 20 ms 3 s

These cover the swarm's own machinery. Most of a task's real time goes to the model and your checks.

docs.title: Real harness runs
docs.text:
Script What it proves scripts/gate2_claude.sh A real Claude Code session finishes 10 tasks over MCP, with no call past 45 seconds scripts/gate3_real.sh ID A real harness finishes tasks through ACP, inside the sandbox ROUTE=mcp scripts/gate_join.sh A real session joins using only what join wrote ROUTE=shell scripts/gate_join.sh The same, for a session already open

These use your harness accounts. gate_join.sh fails if a run finishes through a different route than the one being tested, because that mistake once hid a real bug.

docs.title: From a release
docs.text:
Download the archive for your platform from the project's GitHub releases page, then check it against SHA256SUMS and extract it. Each archive holds the binary, the changelog and the third-party license notices.

Linux and macOSWindows 
sha256sum --check --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS
tar -xzf aiculator_*.tar.gz
sudo mv aiculator_*/aiculator /usr/local/bin/
aiculator --version

Get-FileHash aiculator_*.zip -Algorithm SHA256
Expand-Archive aiculator_*.zip

Then add the extracted folder to your PATH.

Windows is compiled, not yet run

Windows and FreeBSD builds compile, but no one has run them yet. There is no native sandbox on Windows, so sandboxed work needs Docker.

docs.title: From source
docs.text:
You need Go at the version in go.mod, and git.

go install github.com/Grano22/aiculator/cmd/aiculator@latest

Or from a checkout:

CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -ldflags='-s -w' -o bin/aiculator ./cmd/aiculator
export PATH="$PWD/bin:$PATH"

docs.title: Put it on your PATH
docs.text: Skills call aiculator by name, so agents can only use them if it is on your PATH.

docs.title: What else you need
docs.text: Tool When git Always A harness To do any work, such as Claude Code or OpenCode A sandbox To run checks and workers. macOS has one built in. On Linux, install bubblewrap. Elsewhere, use Docker.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: This takes a repository from nothing to one finished, verified task.

docs.title: 1. Connect the project
docs.text:
Run this in a git repository with at least one commit:

aiculator join --tier 1

It does three things, and writes no secrets:

  • Starts a local server, keeping its data in .swarm/, which is excluded from git.
  • Installs the bundled skills into .agents/skills.
  • Adds the swarm's MCP server to the config of each harness it finds.

docs.title: 2. Add a task
docs.text:
aiculator task add \
  --title "Add a health endpoint" \
  --spec "Add GET /healthz returning 200." \
  --check "go test ./..."

The --check command is what decides whether the task is finished. Make sure it fails before the work and passes after it.

docs.title: 3. Get an agent working
docs.text:
A session already openA new sessionA sandboxed worker

Paste this into it:

Read .agents/skills/swarm-join/SKILL.md and follow it. Join as tier 1.

Start your harness in this directory, approve the MCP server if asked, and use the swarm-join skill. In Claude Code, that is /swarm-join.

SWARM_TOKEN=$(aiculator token --agent worker1 --tier 1) \
  aiculator drive --harness claude --agent worker1

docs.title: 4. Watch it finish
docs.text:
aiculator task ls
aiculator situation

The task moves through ready, claimed, running, review and merging to done.

For a live view, run aiculator top in a terminal or aiculator web for your browser. See Dashboards.

docs.title: 5. See the result
docs.text:
Finished work lands on the swarm/integration branch. Your own branches are never touched, so you choose when to merge it:

git log swarm/integration
git merge swarm/integration

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Plan a whole spec instead of adding tasks one at a time.
  • Run sandboxed workers for work you do not fully trust.

docs.title: Dashboards
docs.text: There are two live views of the same data: aiculator top in a terminal, and aiculator web in a browser. Both are read-only.

docs.title: Terminal
docs.text:
aiculator top
Key Action 1 to 5, or tab Switch between overview, tasks, agents, flow and usage ↑ ↓, or j k Scroll p Pause q Quit

Without a terminal, it prints one frame and exits, so it works in scripts:

aiculator top --once --view usage
aiculator top --json | jq '.usage.tokens'

--no-color and NO_COLOR turn color off. Status is always in words as well as color.

docs.title: Web
docs.text:
aiculator web             # Opens your browser
aiculator web --no-open   # Prints the link
aiculator web --ttl 1h    # Expires sooner; the default is 12 hours

It follows your system's light or dark setting, works at phone width, and pauses while its tab is hidden.

The dashboard is a plugin compiled into the binary. go build -tags noweb leaves it out, saving about 0.1 MiB.

docs.title: Flow
docs.text: How many tasks are in each state, and how often tasks have moved between states. Many running → failed moves mean agents are struggling, and merging → failed means merge conflicts.

docs.title: Throughput
docs.text: Rates over the last minute, with per-second history for the last 60 seconds.

docs.title: Latency and jitter
docs.text:
Row Measures What a high value means Queue wait From ready to granted Not enough agents Commit One durable write The disk or the store is struggling API call One call, leaving out long-polls The server is struggling. progress and submit are slower by nature, because they save work with git. Task cycle From created to merged Tasks are slow or retrying

Jitter is how much consecutive samples differ, smoothed the way RFC 3550 does for network jitter. High jitter with a low median points to occasional stalls.

docs.title: Health
docs.text:
Each task holding a lease is one of:

Health Meaning OK Plenty of time left At risk Under a quarter of its lease or progress time remains Expired Past its deadline, and about to be taken back

"Progress left" counts down until the agent must change files. An agent that heartbeats without changing anything runs out of this and is caught as a zombie. Problems sort to the top, and the list holds at most 200 tasks.

Agents are working, waiting, idle or gone, which means not seen for 30 seconds.

docs.title: Probes
docs.text: Probe Checks writer The engine answers store The state store answers event_log The event log is keeping up git The repository and integration branch are readable sandbox Which sandbox checks run in

docs.title: Usage and budgets
docs.text:
Tokens come from harnesses that report them over ACP, or from --tokens and the tokens tool argument. Cost is only what agents report, in micro-dollars, because the swarm does not know your prices. It reads zero when nothing reports it.

Totals by task and tier come from durable state, so they survive a restart. Rates and per-agent figures start again when the server restarts.

docs.title: For other tools
docs.text:
Endpoint Token Use GET /v1/healthz None Is the process up GET /v1/readyz None Is it ready. Returns 503 if a probe fails, with no details. GET /metrics Viewer Prometheus format GET /v1/observe Viewer The full snapshot as JSON GET /v1/events Viewer Every task change, as JSON lines

Create a read-only token for a scraper with the API's /v1/tokens route, setting viewer: true. aiculator web --no-open also prints one in its link.

aiculator events | jq -r 'select(.state == "parked") | "\(.id): \(.reason)"'

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Viewer tokens can read but cannot add tasks, take work or mint tokens.
  • The page and its scripts hold no data, so they need no token. All data does.
  • The link's token sits in the URL fragment, which browsers never send to a server. The page then removes it from the address bar and keeps it only for that tab.
  • A strict content security policy blocks anything from elsewhere and anything inline.
  • Task titles and agent names come from agents, so they are untrusted. The web page only ever renders them as text, and the terminal view strips control characters so they cannot steer your terminal.

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text:
Aiculator's logging works like Kubernetes: -v=0 to -v=9, with --vmodule to raise one component on its own. If you know kubectl -v=8, you already know how to use this.

aiculator task ls -v=6                  # See the HTTP calls this command makes
aiculator up --v=4                      # Start a server with debug logging
aiculator debug verbosity 5 --for 10m   # Trace a running server for ten minutes
aiculator logs -f --component engine    # Follow what it is doing

docs.title: Levels
docs.text:
The levels mean what kubectl's mean. aiculator debug levels prints this list.

Level kubectl's meaning What it shows here 0 Always visible to an operator Errors, and verbosity changes 1 A reasonable default Server start, serious warnings such as a lost planner or a stale revision 2 Steady state; recommended A server's default. Task transitions, plans, MCP tool calls, sessions, merges 3 Changes in detail Every commit and grant, rejected commands and why, permission decisions, checks starting 4 Debug Why an agent was told to wait or exit, worktrees, check output, sandbox commands 5 Trace Every git command, why a task was not eligible, compare-and-swap revisions 6 Requested resources Method, URL, status and time of each HTTP call 7 HTTP headers Also headers, with credentials removed 8 HTTP contents Also bodies, MCP arguments and agent text, cut to 1 KiB, with credentials removed 9 HTTP contents, untruncated Also bodies up to 1 MiB, with credentials removed

A command defaults to 0 and a server to 2. Precedence is the flag, then AICULATOR_V, then the default. All these forms work: -v=6, -v 6, --v=6 and --v 6.

Logs go to stderr, so stdout stays clean for scripts, even at level 9.

docs.title: What it looks like
docs.text:
At level 5 on a server, one task being granted:

level=INFO msg="task created" v=2 component=engine task=fix-login title="Fix the login redirect" tier=1 plan_epoch=0
level=INFO msg=commit v=3 component=engine task=fix-login kind=publish actor=system:plan took=65.542µs
level=INFO msg=compare-and-swap v=5 component=engine task=fix-login from_rev=1 to_rev=2 lease=0
level=INFO msg="task transition" v=2 component=engine task=fix-login from=draft to=ready tier=1 attempt=0 actor=system:plan reason=""
level=INFO msg=commit v=3 component=engine task=fix-login kind=grant actor=worker1 took=59.333µs
level=INFO msg=compare-and-swap v=5 component=engine task=fix-login from_rev=2 to_rev=3 lease=1
level=INFO msg="task transition" v=2 component=engine task=fix-login from=ready to=claimed tier=1 attempt=1 actor=worker1 reason=""

At level 6 on a command:

level=INFO msg=request v=6 component=client method=GET url=http://127.0.0.1:7777/v1/tasks status=200 took=752.833µs bytes=412

At level 8, asking for a token. The caller gets the token on stdout, and the log shows none of it:

level=INFO msg="request headers" v=7 component=client method=POST path=/v1/tokens headers="Authorization: [redacted]; Content-Type: application/json"
level=INFO msg="request body" v=8 component=client method=POST path=/v1/tokens body="{\"agent\":\"demo\",\"tier\":1}"
level=INFO msg=request v=6 component=client method=POST url=http://127.0.0.1:7777/v1/tokens status=200 took=736.75µs bytes=134
level=INFO msg="response headers" v=7 component=client path=/v1/tokens headers="Content-Length: 134; Content-Type: application/json; Date: ..."
level=INFO msg="response body" v=8 component=client path=/v1/tokens status=200 body="{\"token\":\"[redacted]\"}"

docs.title: One component at a time
docs.text:
Raising everything to 5 is noisy. --vmodule sets a level per component, can use wildcards, and can also lower one:

aiculator up --vmodule engine=5,work=4
aiculator up --v=5 --vmodule http=0

The components are engine, work, driver, swarm, sandbox, mcp, http, client and store.

docs.title: On a running server
docs.text:
No restart is needed, and anything in progress carries on:

aiculator debug verbosity                        # Show the current setting
aiculator debug verbosity 5 --for 10m            # Trace, then go back by itself
aiculator debug verbosity --vmodule engine=5 --for 5m
aiculator debug verbosity 2                      # Change it for good

Use --for. It means a debugging session cannot leave a server logging heavily because someone forgot. Changing the level needs the admin token, and the change itself is logged.

docs.title: Reading the logs
docs.text:
aiculator logs reads the log of a server started with aiculator up:

aiculator logs --tail 50
aiculator logs -f --component engine
aiculator logs -f --grep fix-login

For other tools, --log-format json writes one JSON object per line, and --log-file PATH writes to a file:

aiculator logs -f | grep 'task transition'
aiculator up --log-format json --v=3

aiculator top never writes logs to the screen, because they would corrupt it. Use --log-file to capture them.

docs.title: Common problems
docs.text: Question Try Why does this task never start? aiculator debug verbosity --vmodule engine=5 --for 2m, then look for not eligible. It names the tier, tags and file conflict. Why does this agent keep waiting? At level 4, wait answered gives the action and reason Why was a command refused? At level 3, command rejected gives the state and reason Why did the checks fail? At level 4, check output holds what the command printed What is git doing? At level 5, git lists each command and how long it took Why was a tool call denied? At level 3 on the driver, permission decision gives the tool and kind What is this client sending? -v=8 on the command

docs.title: What is safe to share
docs.text:
Credentials are removed where lines are written, so no call site can leak one by mistake. Tests read the logs at level 9 on both the client and the server, after real calls over HTTP and MCP, and fail if a token appears. Anything named like a credential is removed, as is anything shaped like a token or a bearer header, wherever it appears.

Levels 8 and 9 show content

Task titles, specs, notes and agent messages all appear. Credentials are removed, but your code and instructions may be in there, so read a level 8 or 9 log before sharing it.

The log file is not rotated

.swarm/server.log grows as long as the server runs. Level 9 fills it quickly, which is another reason to use --for.

A disabled log call costs about 2 ns and allocates nothing, so debug logging can stay in the hottest paths.

docs.title: Join from an open harness
docs.text: You can turn a harness session into a swarm worker at any time, including one that was open before the swarm existed.

docs.title: Set up once per project
docs.text:
aiculator join --tier 1

Name harnesses with --harness claude,opencode. Without it, every harness found on your PATH is set up. To allow planning as well, add --planner.

docs.title: Choose a route
docs.text:
Route Needs a restart? Works for How Shell No Any harness that can run commands Paste the line below MCP Yes, MCP loads at session start Harnesses with a project MCP file Use the swarm-join skill

The line to paste into a session that is already open:

Read .agents/skills/swarm-join/SKILL.md and follow it. Join as tier 1.

The skill checks whether the session has the swarm's tools. If it does not, it uses aiculator work commands instead. Pi and goose always use this route.

docs.title: What a joined session can do
docs.text:
Both routes offer the same operations:

Operation MCP tool Shell command Get the next task wait_for_task aiculator work wait Take a specific task claim aiculator work claim Extend the lease heartbeat aiculator work heartbeat Save work progress aiculator work progress Finish submit aiculator work submit Give up fail aiculator work fail Hand back with no penalty release aiculator work release Review another agent's work review_verdict aiculator work verdict See the swarm situation aiculator work situation

A session joined with --planner also gets plan_begin, plan_update, plan_add and plan_commit. See Plan work.

docs.title: What the answers mean
docs.text:
Each wait returns an action:

  • task: you hold a lease on that task, and workdir is where to do it.
  • wait: nothing yet, and reason says why: planning, planner_lost, deps, tier_busy or idle.
  • exit: no more work can reach this tier.

A joined session is not sandboxed

It runs under your harness's own permissions. In one test, a model started its own server in a temp directory on its own initiative. The acceptance checks still run in the sandbox, but for work you do not fully trust, use sandboxed workers.

OpenCode 2

A running OpenCode background service does not pick up new project config, and opencode mcp list shows the service's view. Use opencode run --standalone or restart the service. The shell route works either way.

docs.title: Undo
docs.text:
aiculator unjoin

This removes the swarm's MCP entries and skill links, and nothing else. Add --purge to delete the swarm's skills from .agents/skills too.

docs.title: MCP config
docs.text: aiculator join sets up MCP for you. These commands give you direct control, for one harness or any config file.

docs.title: Add
docs.text:
aiculator mcp add                               # Every installed harness
aiculator mcp add --harness opencode --tier 2   # By id
aiculator mcp add --harness claude,cursor --global
aiculator mcp add --harness ~/.local/bin/opencode   # Found from its executable
aiculator mcp add --harness ./custom/mcp.json   # A config file; format inferred
aiculator mcp add --harness opencode --dry-run  # Show it; change nothing

--harness accepts auto, all, harness ids, a path to a harness's executable, or a path to a config file. For a config file, the format comes from its name: .toml means Codex's format, opencode* means OpenCode's, and anything else is the common mcpServers JSON. Override it with --format.

docs.title: Print the config piece
docs.text:
To add it by hand, print it. This changes nothing.

$ aiculator mcp print --harness opencode
# opencode: add to opencode.json
{
  "mcp": {
    "servers": {
      "swarm": {
        "command": [
          "aiculator",
          "mcp",
          "--auto",
          "--tier",
          "1",
          "--harness",
          "opencode"
        ],
        "timeout": {
          "execution": 60000
        },
        "type": "local"
      }
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Any other server
docs.text:
These commands manage any MCP server, not only the swarm's. Give it a name and put its command after --:

aiculator mcp add --name docs --harness claude -- npx -y docs-server
aiculator mcp print --name docs --harness codex -- npx -y docs-server
aiculator mcp add --name api --env API_URL=https://x --harness cursor -- api-server

--env values are stored in plain text

Do not put real secrets in a file you commit.

docs.title: Remove
docs.text:
aiculator mcp remove --harness opencode                # The swarm's entry
aiculator mcp remove --harness opencode --name docs    # A named one

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
• The swarm's entry holds no token. The bridge, aiculator mcp --auto, gets its own when it starts, so these files are safe to commit.
  • Your other settings stay. Each change is merged, and the previous file is saved in .swarm/backups/.
  • A file it cannot understand is left alone. That includes invalid JSON and opencode.jsonc, which may hold comments. You get the piece to paste instead.
  • Timeouts are set for you. The wait_for_task call can hold for up to 40 seconds, so the entry allows 60.

docs.title: Plan work
docs.text: A plan turns a spec into many tasks, and keeps waiting workers informed while that happens. The swarm-plan skill walks a model through it, or you can drive it by hand.

docs.title: The steps
docs.text:
# 1. Take the lease BEFORE reading the spec. Workers now wait instead of exiting.
aiculator plan begin --ttl 5m          # Prints the epoch

# 2. Renew it as you go, and tell workers what you are doing.
aiculator plan update --epoch 1 --ttl 5m --phase "reading code"

# 3. Publish what is coming.
aiculator plan update --epoch 1 --ttl 5m --phase splitting --expected 1=12 --expected 2=3

# 4. Add tasks. Workers cannot see them yet.
aiculator plan add --epoch 1 --id api --title "Add the API" --tier 2 --check "go test ./api"
aiculator plan add --epoch 1 --id ui --title "Add the UI" --dep api --check "npm test"

# 5. Publish the whole plan at once.
aiculator plan commit --epoch 1

docs.title: What workers see
docs.text:
{
  "action": "wait",
  "reason": "planning",
  "planning": {
    "epoch": 1,
    "phase": "splitting",
    "expected_tasks": {"1": 12, "2": 3},
    "age_ms": 180,
    "stale": false
  }
}

docs.title: Rules the swarm enforces
docs.text:
• A hint is a promise. Agents may exit once nothing is expected at or below their tier. After that, the swarm refuses tasks and hint changes that would have reached them.
  • One planner at a time. A second one is refused while the lease is live.
  • A crashed planner cannot do damage. If the lease expires, its drafts are canceled, the epoch rises, and its old epoch is refused. Waiting workers see planner_lost.
  • A plan cannot deadlock. Commit rejects dependency cycles and unknown dependencies.

docs.title: Writing good tasks
docs.text:
• Start low on the tier. Failures escalate automatically.
  • Always give a --check that fails before the work and passes after it.
  • Declare --touches path, so that overlapping tasks do not run at the same time.
  • Keep tasks small, because a worker sees only its own spec and the code.

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text:
There are three ways to extend Aiculator, depending on how much you need.

Way Needs a rebuild? Can do Use it for Event stream No Read every task change Notifications, logs, in any language Program on PATH No Add a command Your own tools Compiled in Yes Add commands, server routes and event handlers Features that ship inside the binary

docs.title: List what you have
docs.text:
$ aiculator plugin
NAME     KIND         DESCRIPTION
webdash  compiled in  Web dashboard, embedded in the binary

docs.title: Event stream
docs.text:
aiculator events | while read -r line; do
  echo "$line" | jq -r 'select(.state == "done") | .id' | xargs -I{} notify-send "Done: {}"
done

docs.title: A program on PATH
docs.text:
Any executable named aiculator-NAME runs as aiculator NAME, the way git does it. It receives AICULATOR_DATA and AICULATOR_VERSION.

#!/bin/sh
# Save as aiculator-greet, somewhere on your PATH.
echo "Hello from $AICULATOR_VERSION"

Built-in commands always win, so a program cannot replace one. Only PATH is searched, so cloning a repository cannot add a command.

docs.title: A compiled-in plugin
docs.text:
Plugins compile in because Go's dynamic plugin package needs cgo, and this binary is static.

A plugin registers itself and implements up to two interfaces:

examples/plugins/hello/hello.go
package hello

import (
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "sync/atomic"

    "github.com/spf13/cobra"

    "github.com/Grano22/aiculator/pkg/plugin"
)

type Plugin struct{}

func init() { plugin.Register(Plugin{}) }

func (Plugin) Name() string        { return "hello" }
func (Plugin) Description() string { return "Example plugin that counts finished tasks" }

// Setup runs once in the server.
func (Plugin) Setup(h *plugin.Host) error {
    var done atomic.Int64
    h.OnEvent(func(e plugin.Event) {
        if e.State == "done" {
            done.Add(1)
        }
    })
    h.HandleViewer("count", http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, _ *http.Request) {
        fmt.Fprintf(w, "%d\n", done.Load())
    }))
    return nil
}

// Commands is optional, and adds CLI commands.
func (Plugin) Commands(cli *plugin.CLI) []*cobra.Command {
    return []*cobra.Command{{
        Use:   "hello",
        Short: "Say how many tasks are done",
        RunE: func(cmd *cobra.Command, _ []string) error {
            s, err := cli.Snapshot(cmd.Context())
            if err != nil {
                return err
            }
            fmt.Printf("Hello. %d tasks are done.\n", s.States["done"])
            return nil
        },
    }}
}

Include it with a small file in cmd/aiculator, in your own fork:

cmd/aiculator/plugins_hello.go
//go:build example_hello

package main

import _ "github.com/Grano22/aiculator/examples/plugins/hello"

Then build with its tag:

go build -tags example_hello ./cmd/aiculator

Leave out the build tag line if it should always be included. The web dashboard works the opposite way: it is in by default, and -tags noweb removes it.

docs.title: What a plugin can do
docs.text: Method Purpose h.Handle(path, handler) A route with no token, for what anyone on this machine may read, such as static files h.HandleViewer(path, handler) A route that needs a viewer or admin token h.OnEvent(fn) Be told about every task change h.Snapshot(ctx) Read the live dashboard data h.Log Log with the plugin's name attached Commands(cli) Add CLI commands, and use cli.Snapshot and cli.ViewerToken

docs.title: What the swarm guarantees
docs.text:
• A plugin cannot take the server down. One that fails or panics in setup is disabled alone, and a panic in a handler fails only that request or event.
  • A slow plugin cannot slow the swarm. Events are dropped for it rather than waited on, so delivery is best effort.
  • Routes stay in their own space, under /plugins/NAME/, so a plugin cannot shadow the API or another plugin.
  • A command cannot replace a built-in. It is skipped, with a warning.

Compiled-in plugins are fully trusted

A plugin is ordinary Go code in your process, and these guarantees are about mistakes, not malice. Read a plugin before you build it in.

pkg/plugin and pkg/observe are the public API. They may still change before version 1.0.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text:
Skills live in one place, .agents/skills/, the cross-client convention from agentskills.io. Harnesses that scan it need nothing, and the rest get a symlink, so an edit reaches all of them.

.agents, plural

Harnesses scan .agents/skills, so that is the main location. Skills in .agent/skills are picked up too, and linked across.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
aiculator skill --install '*'                   # All skills, to every installed harness
aiculator skill --install 'swarm-*' '*-tool'    # By pattern
aiculator skill --install '*' --global          # ~/.agents/skills and home directories
aiculator skill --install '*' --harness all     # Every supported harness
aiculator skill --install x --harness claude,pi
aiculator skill --install x --path ./vendor/skills --harness none
aiculator skill --install x --source ~/my-skills
aiculator skill --install x --copy              # Copy, for tools that do not follow links

Patterns use * for anything, ? for one character and [abc] for a set.

Quote your patterns

A bare * works: the shell expands it into the directory listing, and aiculator recognizes that exact list as "all". But zsh stops with an error on an unmatched *-sth before aiculator runs, so quote anything else.

docs.title: Manage
docs.text:
aiculator skill --list                # Versions, lint state and who can see what
aiculator skill --lint                # Check against the Agent Skills spec
aiculator skill --new my-skill --description "..."
aiculator skill --uninstall 'swarm-*'           # Remove links; keep the source
aiculator skill --uninstall 'swarm-*' --purge   # Also delete the source

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
• Your own directories are never replaced, even with --force.
  • A skill that fails the linter is not linked anywhere.
  • Reinstalling keeps your edits to a bundled skill. --force restores the bundled version.

docs.title: Bundled skills
docs.text: Skill Use swarm-join Work the queue. It only starts when you ask for it. swarm-plan Turn a spec into tasks. swarm-operate Start the server, add tasks, launch workers.

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text:
Use the spec's fields first. These are understood everywhere:

---
name: my-skill              # Must match the directory
description: What it does and when to use it, in words people actually use.
license: MIT
compatibility: Requires git and internet access.
allowed-tools: Read Bash(git:*)
metadata:                   # String values only, so quote numbers
  version: "1.0.0"
---

Some fields work only in certain harnesses. Others ignore them, so they are safe in project skills, but claude.ai uploads and the Skills API reject them.

Field or file Honored by disable-model-invocation Claude Code, Cursor, Pi paths Claude Code, Cursor when_to_use, argument-hint, arguments, user-invocable, disallowed-tools, model, effort, context, agent, hooks Claude Code icon, color Cursor agents/openai.yaml Codex

aiculator skill --lint explains each of these when it finds one.

docs.title: Template demo
docs.text:
One template that uses every template feature, in a realistic workflow: shipping a feature, from choosing an approach to opening the pull request.

Source: .agent/template/demo.mdx

Always current: both the source and the output below are included from the real files, and a test fails if a new component is not used in the demo.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
aiculator template --render demo                 # (1)!
aiculator template --render demo --for claude    # (2)!
aiculator template --render demo --set retries=5 # (3)!
aiculator template --install demo                # (4)!
  1. Prints the skill and writes nothing.
  2. Shows what one harness's own copy looks like, naming its real question tool.
  3. Overrides a default from the template's vars.
  4. Writes it to .agents/skills/demo, and links it to each installed harness that needs a link.

Run this from a checkout of this repository

demo.mdx lives in this repository's .agent/template, so it is not bundled in the binary. To use it elsewhere, copy the .agent/template directory into your project.

docs.title: How it renders
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["demo.mdx, your template"] --> B["Jinja2: variables, conditions, loops, includes"]

docs.text:
The rendered skill leads a model through this conversation:

sequenceDiagram
    actor U as You
    participant M as Orchestrator
    participant S as Subagents

    M->>U: Free text: what is it called?
    U-->>M: faster-checkout
    M->>U: Single choice: which approach?
    U-->>M: Smallest change
    M->>U: Previews: which API style?
    U-->>M: Options object
    M->>U: Checkboxes: which checks?
    U-->>M: Unit tests, lint
    M->>U: Tabs: rollout and docs
    U-->>M: Both answered

    U-->>M: Approved

What it renders to
docs.text:
The same template, per harness. Compare "Track the work" and "Step F" across these tabs: each names what that harness really has.

Claude Code OpenCode Pi Shared

Names AskUserQuestion, TaskCreate and EnterPlanMode.

aiculator template --render demo --for claude
---

compatibility: Works in any harness that reads skills. These are instructions to the model, not technical limits.

# Ship a feature in the checkout service

## Contents

- Track the work: line 46, anchor `track-work`
- Step A: name the feature: line 70, anchor `name-feature`
- Step B: choose an approach: line 84, anchor `choose-approach`
- Step C: choose the API style: line 106, anchor `choose-api`
- Step D: choose the checks: line 127, anchor `choose-checks`
- Step E: settle the details: line 150, anchor `choose-settings`
- Step F: get the plan approved: line 172, anchor `approve-plan`
- Subagents: line 189, anchor `subagents`
- Step G: build it: research, build, review: line 200, anchor `build-flow`
- Commands: timeouts and retries: line 244, anchor `backoff`
- Checks to run: line 261, anchor `checks`
- Flow: ship it: line 268, anchor `ship-flow`
- Step H: clean up: line 292, anchor `delete-branch`
- Output format: line 307, anchor `output-format`
- Progress: line 318, anchor `progress`
- Release notes: line 332, anchor `changelog`
- How to format your replies: line 343, anchor `formatting`

Rendered for Claude Code, whose question tool is `AskUserQuestion`.

> **MUST** `ship-safely`: Never push to the main branch. Every change goes through a review.

> **MUST NOT** `no-false-claims`: Say something works unless you ran it and saw it work.

> **Note:** This skill is a demo of the template features, built around a realistic workflow.

House style for the checkout service: small commits, plain language, and a test for every fix.

> **CUSTOM COMPONENT:** This one comes from `components/DemoBadge.md`, next to this template.

## Track the work
<!-- anchor: track-work -->

Keep a visible task list for this work, so that the user can see where things stand without asking.

Use `TaskCreate` to add each step and `TaskUpdate` to change its status. Claude Code shows the list live. On some models these tools must be switched on, so if you do not have them, use the fallback below.

- Create the list before you start, with one item per step the user would recognize.
- Mark an item in progress when you begin it, and done as soon as it is finished, never in batches at the end.
- Keep exactly one item in progress at a time.
- If the plan changes, change the list in the same step.

Start with these items:

- Settle the details with the user
- Get the plan approved
- Build and review it
- Open the pull request

Two exceptions:

- **If you have no task list tool:** keep a Markdown checklist (`- [ ]` and `- [x]`) and repeat it whenever it changes.
- **If you are a subagent:** keep your list short, and include its final state in your report.

## Step A: name the feature
<!-- anchor: name-feature -->

**Ask the user:** What should this feature's flag and branch be called?

This needs the user's own words, such as a name, a path or a description, which a list of options cannot offer.

Ask in your reply, as one clear question, and end your turn. `AskUserQuestion` is built for choices, so use it only if a few likely answers are worth offering, since it always lets the user type their own.
Give an example of the form you want: faster-checkout

- Ask for one thing at a time, and say what you will do with the answer.
- If you can find the answer yourself, do that instead of asking.
- **If you are a subagent:** you cannot reach the user. Report what you need, and why.

## Step B: choose an approach
<!-- anchor: choose-approach -->

**Ask the user:** How should I build this feature?

Show this as a single-choice list that the user selects from, not as a question in your reply.

Use the `AskUserQuestion` tool. It takes 1 to 4 questions, each with a `header` of at most 12 characters and 2 to 4 options. Each option has a `label` of 1 to 5 words and a `description`. It adds an "Other" choice by itself, so do not add one.
Set `multiSelect: false`, so that exactly one option can be chosen.

Offer these options:

- Smallest change (Recommended): touch as little as possible
- Refactor first: clean the area up, then add the feature
- Feature flag: ship it switched off

- Put the option you recommend first, and add "(Recommended)" to its label.
- Options must exclude each other. If several could be true together, this is the wrong question type.
- After asking, stop and wait. Do not assume an answer or carry on without one.
- **If you have no question tool:** write a numbered list, ask for one number, and end your turn.
- **If you are a subagent:** you cannot reach the user. Use the smallest change that works, and say so in your report.

## Step C: choose the API style
<!-- anchor: choose-api -->

**Ask the user:** Which API style reads best here?

The options look different and the user has to see them to choose, such as layouts, code styles or output formats. Show each one.

Use the `AskUserQuestion` tool. It takes 1 to 4 questions, each with a `header` of at most 12 characters and 2 to 4 options. Each option has a `label` of 1 to 5 words and a `description`. It adds an "Other" choice by itself, so do not add one.
If the tool offers a `preview` field on its options, put each option's example there. Previews need a single-choice question. Whether this field is offered depends on the session's settings.

Offer these options:

- Options object: `pay({ amount, currency })`
- Plain arguments: `pay(amount, currency)`

- Make each preview real: a code snippet, a small ASCII mockup or a sample of the output.
- Keep previews about the same length, so that they compare fairly.
- **If the tool has no previews:** put each option in your reply, under its own label with its example in a code block, and then ask which one the user wants.
- After asking, stop and wait.
- **If you are a subagent:** choose the option that best fits the task, and report your choice with its example.

## Step D: choose the checks
<!-- anchor: choose-checks -->

**Ask the user:** Which checks should I run before review?

Show this as a checkbox list, where the user can tick any number of options, not as a question in your reply.

Use the `AskUserQuestion` tool. It takes 1 to 4 questions, each with a `header` of at most 12 characters and 2 to 4 options. Each option has a `label` of 1 to 5 words and a `description`. It adds an "Other" choice by itself, so do not add one.
Set `multiSelect: true`, so that several options can be chosen.

Offer these options:

- Unit tests
- Lint
- Security scan

- Phrase the question so that choosing several makes sense, such as "Which of these should I include?"
- At least 1 must be chosen. If fewer are, ask again.
- Options must be independent, so that any combination is valid. If some exclude each other, ask them separately.
- After asking, stop and wait. Do not assume an answer or carry on without one.
- **If you have no question tool, or it has no multi-select:** write a numbered list, ask for all the numbers that apply, separated by commas, and end your turn.
- **If you are a subagent:** you cannot reach the user. Choose only what the task clearly requires, and report those choices to the agent that started you.

## Step E: settle the details
<!-- anchor: choose-settings -->

Ask related questions together in a **single call**, so that they appear as tabs the user can move between before submitting. Do not ask them one at a time, and do not ask them in your reply.

Use the `AskUserQuestion` tool. It takes 1 to 4 questions, each with a `header` of at most 12 characters and 2 to 4 options. Each option has a `label` of 1 to 5 words and a `description`. It adds an "Other" choice by itself, so do not add one.
Put every question in the `questions` array of one call, each with its own short `header`, which is the tab's label. Set `multiSelect` for each question on its own.

Ask these:

- **Rollout**: How should it roll out? *(one can be chosen)*
  All at once (Recommended), or gradually

- **Docs**: Which docs need updating? *(several can be chosen)*
  README, or the changelog, or the API reference

- Ask at most 4 together. For more, group the related ones and make a second call only after the first is answered.

Ask related questions together in a **single call**, so that they appear as tabs the user can move between before submitting. Do not ask them one at a time, and do not ask them in your reply.

Use your harness's question tool if it has one: `AskUserQuestion` in Claude Code, `question` in OpenCode, `ask_user` in Gemini CLI.
Put every question in one call, each with its own short header, which is the tab's label.

Ask these:

- **Rollout**: How should it roll out? *(one can be chosen)*
  All at once (Recommended), or gradually

- **Docs**: Which docs need updating? *(several can be chosen)*
  README, or the changelog, or the API reference

- Ask at most 4 together. For more, group the related ones and make a second call only after the first is answered.
- Each question must stand on its own, because the user may answer them in any order.
- After asking, stop and wait for all the answers. Do not assume any of them.
- **If you have no question tool:** write the questions as numbered sections with lettered options, ask for answers in the form `1: a, 2: b c`, and end your turn.
- **If you are a subagent:** you cannot reach the user. Answer each one with the recommended option, and report your choices to the agent that started you.

## Step F: get the plan approved
<!-- anchor: approve-plan -->

Do not change anything until the user has approved a plan.

Use your harness's plan mode if it has one: `EnterPlanMode` and `ExitPlanMode` in Claude Code, `enter_plan_mode` and `exit_plan_mode` in Gemini CLI.

The plan must cover:

- The answers from steps A to E
- The checks you will run, and in what order

- Say which files will change, how you will verify the result, and what could go wrong.
- If the user asks for changes, revise the plan and ask again. Do not start on a partial approval.
- **If you have no plan mode:** write the plan as a numbered list, ask for approval, and end your turn.
- **If you are a subagent:** you cannot get approval, so report your plan and change nothing, unless your task says to make the changes.

## Subagents
<!-- anchor: subagents -->

Decide per piece of work, using these rules. If neither rule applies, do the work yourself.

- **Use a subagent when:** the work splits into independent parts, or needs broad searching
- **Do not use a subagent when:** the steps depend on each other
- **Run at most 3 at once.** Wait for one to finish before starting another.

If your harness has no way to run subagents, do the work in order yourself and say so once.

## Step G: build it: research, build, review
<!-- anchor: build-flow -->

You are the orchestrator. Run the stages below in order, and delegate each one to a subagent. Keep your own work to coordinating and checking results, so that your context stays clear.

- **Give each subagent everything it needs.** It starts with none of this conversation, so its prompt must state the goal, the inputs, the exact output you want, and when to stop.
- **Do not guess a subagent's result.** Wait for it, read it, and check it against the stage's "Done when" before moving on.
- **Run a stage in parallel only if it says so.** Parallel subagents must not change the same files.
- **Subagents cannot reach the user.** Questions that need the user are for you to ask between stages. A subagent makes a reasonable choice, and reports it.
- **If a stage fails,** retry it once with what you learned added to the prompt. If it fails again, stop and report what happened, rather than continuing on a bad result.
- **If your harness cannot run subagents,** do each stage yourself, in order, and say so once.

### Stage 1: Research
<!-- anchor: research -->

**Run up to 3 subagents at once.**

Find the code this feature touches.

**Output:** Short findings with file paths, and no changes to any file

**Done when:** you could explain the change, with evidence for each claim

### Stage 2: Build
<!-- anchor: build -->

Make the change the user chose in step B.

**Output:** The changes made, and how they were checked

**Done when:** the code is changed and the tests pass

### Stage 3: Review
<!-- anchor: review -->

**Subagent:** a fresh subagent that did not write the code
Look for bugs in the changes.

**Output:** Real problems, each with a file, a line and why it matters

**Done when:** each problem is fixed, or you have explained why it stays

When every stage is done, combine the results and report them yourself. Never pass a subagent's text on unchecked.

## Commands: timeouts and retries
<!-- anchor: backoff -->

Give every command a time limit of **120s**. A command that hits the limit has failed; do not wait longer.

Retry only for: timeouts, network errors and rate limits.
Do not retry a failure that will repeat, such as a failing test, a syntax error or a denied permission. Read the error and change something first.

| Attempt | Wait before it |
|---|---|
| 1 | None |
| 2 | 2s |
| 3 | 4s |
| 4 | 8s |

After the last attempt, stop retrying. Report the command, the final error and what you tried.

## Checks to run
<!-- anchor: checks -->

1. Run unit tests, and stop if it fails.
2. Run lint, and stop if it fails.
3. Run security scan, and stop if it fails.

## Flow: ship it
<!-- anchor: ship-flow -->

Do these steps in order, one at a time. Do not skip a step or merge steps, except as stated here. After each step, say which step you finished and which comes next.

- **Steps marked "Ask the user":** ask, then stop and wait for the answer. Use your harness's question tool if it has one, and otherwise end your turn with the question. Do not guess the answer or continue without it.
- **If you are a subagent:** you were started by another agent and cannot reach the user. Follow the "As a subagent" line in each step instead of asking. Report every default you chose to the agent that started you.

### Step 1: Confirm
<!-- anchor: confirm -->

Summarize what changed and what you checked.

**Ask the user:** Is this ready to ship?

**As a subagent:** Do not ask. Report that it is ready, with your evidence.

### Step 2: Ship
<!-- anchor: ship -->

Open the pull request.

**As a subagent:** Do not ship. Only the agent that started you does that.

## Step H: clean up
<!-- anchor: delete-branch -->

**Ask the user:** Delete the merged feature branch?

Ask this as a yes or no choice, and do not continue until you have the answer.

Use your harness's question tool if it has one: `AskUserQuestion` in Claude Code, `question` in OpenCode, `ask_user` in Gemini CLI.
Offer two options: the action, named specifically, and a way to decline.

- Name what will happen in the option itself, such as "Delete 3 branches", not just "Yes".
- Say what cannot be undone.
- Silence is not a yes. If the answer is unclear, ask again.
- **If you have no question tool:** ask for a clear yes or no, and end your turn.
- **If you are a subagent:** do not take the action. Report that it needs confirmation.

## Output format
<!-- anchor: output-format -->

Every reply must use exactly this format, including short ones and replies late in a long session. Before you send a reply, compare it with this format and fix any difference.

```text
Done: what changed
Checked: what you ran and the result
Next: what remains, or "nothing"
```

## Progress
<!-- anchor: progress -->

**This section is alive: keep it true.** Update it after each step above. Treat a stale section as a bug.

- Change only what lies between the markers, and leave the markers themselves in place.
- Replace what is out of date instead of adding to it, so that this always reads as the present state and never as a history.
- It must always cover: the current step, and anything blocking it.
- If you are a subagent, report what should change to the agent that started you, unless you were told to edit it.

<!-- dynamic:progress:start -->
Not started.
<!-- dynamic:progress:end -->

## Release notes
<!-- anchor: changelog -->

**This section is alive: keep it true.** Update it whenever the plan changes. Treat a stale section as a bug.

It lives in `RELEASE_NOTES.md`, between the marker comments `<!-- dynamic:changelog:start -->` and `<!-- dynamic:changelog:end -->`. Create the file and markers if they do not exist yet.

- Change only what lies between the markers, and leave the markers themselves in place.
- Replace what is out of date instead of adding to it, so that this always reads as the present state and never as a history.
- If you are a subagent, report what should change to the agent that started you, unless you were told to edit it.

## How to format your replies
<!-- anchor: formatting -->

Choose the form that makes each thing easiest to read, using the rules below. Do not decorate: a short answer in a plain sentence is often best, and formatting should never replace a clear explanation.

This output goes to a terminal. Assume code blocks and tables work, and that diagrams, images, collapsible sections and LaTeX may not.

### Code
<!-- anchor: render-code -->

Put all code in a fenced block with a language, so that it is highlighted and easy to copy. Never indent it instead. Say which file it belongs to on the line above.

````markdown
In `internal/calc.go`:

```go
func add(a, b int) int { return a + b }
```
````

### Names in text
<!-- anchor: render-inline -->

Put file names, commands, flags, functions and values in `inline code`. Use **bold** only for the one thing the reader must not miss, *italics* rarely, and ~~strikethrough~~ only for something explicitly withdrawn.

### Commands
<!-- anchor: render-shell -->

Give commands in a `sh` block that can be pasted as it is: no `$` prompt, and one step per line. Show their output in a separate `text` block. Say beforehand if a command changes anything.

```sh
go test ./...
```

### Changes
<!-- anchor: render-diff -->

To show a change to code, use a `diff` block with just enough context to place it.

```diff
-func add(a, b int) int { return a - b }
+func add(a, b int) int { return a + b }
```

### Tables
<!-- anchor: render-table -->

Use a table to compare items across two or more attributes. Keep cells to a few words, put explanations in the text around it, and right-align numbers. Do not use a table for a plain list, or for one row.

```markdown
| Option | Speed | Cost |
|---|--:|--:|
| A | 12 ms | $3 |
| B | 40 ms | $1 |
```

### Lists
<!-- anchor: render-list -->

Use a numbered list when order matters, and bullets when it does not. Keep items parallel and short. A list of one item should be a sentence, and do not nest deeper than two levels.

### Checklists
<!-- anchor: render-checklist -->

Show progress or remaining steps as a checklist.

```markdown
- [x] Add the endpoint
- [ ] Write the tests
```

### Headings
<!-- anchor: render-headings -->

Use `##` and `###` to divide longer answers into parts a reader can scan. Do not skip levels. A short answer needs no heading, and it should open with the answer, not with a heading.

### Callouts
<!-- anchor: render-callout -->

Set off a warning or key note as a quote, starting with a bold label. Use this only for what the reader must not miss, and rarely.

```markdown
> **Warning:** This deletes the production table.
```

### Quotes
<!-- anchor: render-quote -->

Quote errors, logs and documents exactly. Use a `text` code block for machine output, and a `>` quote for what a person or document said.

### File trees
<!-- anchor: render-tree -->

Show a directory layout in a `text` block, using box-drawing characters.

```text
cmd/
├── main.go
└── serve.go
```

### Links
<!-- anchor: render-link -->

Write links as `[what it is](https://example.com)`, with text that says where they go, not "here". Only link to URLs you have actually seen, and do not invent them.

### Diagrams
<!-- anchor: render-diagram -->

A terminal may show Mermaid as plain source, so draw flows as ASCII in a `text` block. Use a Mermaid block only when the user asks, or when the answer is going into a document that renders it.

```text
Request --> Valid? --yes--> Save
              |
              no--> Reject
```

### Images
<!-- anchor: render-image -->

A terminal may not show images, so give the file's path and say what it shows. Do not rely on an image to carry the point.

### Collapsible sections
<!-- anchor: render-details -->

A terminal may show `<details>` tags as plain text, so do not use them. Leave optional material out and offer it, or put it at the end under its own heading.

### Math
<!-- anchor: render-math -->

A terminal may show LaTeX as plain source, so write formulas in plain text or a code block, such as `p99 = sorted[n * 99 / 100]`.

### Footnotes and sources
<!-- anchor: render-footnote -->

A terminal may not render footnotes, so put an aside in its own short sentence, and cite sources as links at the point they are used.

### Horizontal rules
<!-- anchor: render-rule -->

Use a `---` rule only between truly separate parts of a reply. Headings usually do this better.

### File references
<!-- anchor: render-fileref -->

Refer to code as `path/to/file.go:42`, with the line number, because many harnesses make this clickable. Use the path from the project root, and do not wrap it in a link.

In this demo, cite the checkout code this way in every review finding.
